questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working the problem, forming a full acetal from one mole of an aldehyde consumes how many moles of alcohol?
questions.explanation: Conversion of an aldehyde to an acetal replaces the carbonyl oxygen with two alkoxy groups, so two moles of alcohol are consumed and one mole of water is produced.
questions.hint: Two alkoxy groups require two alcohol molecules.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count oxygen atoms in the byproduct
questions.stem: Working the problem, the Wittig reaction produces triphenylphosphine oxide as a byproduct. How many oxygen atoms does this byproduct contain?
questions.explanation: Triphenylphosphine oxide contains one oxygen bonded to phosphorus; that oxygen is originally the carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde or ketone.
questions.hint: The carbonyl oxygen ends up on phosphorus.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working the problem, condensation of one mole of a ketone with one mole of a primary amine releases how many moles of water?
questions.explanation: Imine formation removes two hydrogens from nitrogen and one oxygen from the carbonyl as a single molecule of water, so one mole of water is released per mole of imine.
questions.hint: One condensation releases one water.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count substituents on an aldehyde carbonyl
questions.stem: Working the problem, how many alkyl or carbon substituents are attached to the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde?
questions.explanation: Acetaldehyde has one methyl group and one hydrogen attached to the carbonyl carbon, so it bears a single carbon substituent, which is why it is more reactive than a ketone.
questions.hint: Aldehydes bear one carbon group.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the formula, reducing one mole of a ketone with sodium borohydride consumes how many moles of hydride formally transferred to carbonyl carbons?
questions.explanation: Each ketone molecule accepts one hydride at its carbonyl carbon, so one mole of ketone consumes one mole of hydride equivalents even though borohydride can deliver four hydrides per mole of reagent.
questions.hint: One hydride per carbonyl group.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count carbon groups after Grignard addition
questions.stem: For the formula, adding methylmagnesium bromide to acetone gives a tertiary alcohol. How many methyl groups surround the carbinol carbon?
questions.explanation: Acetone contributes two methyl groups on the carbonyl carbon and the Grignard adds a third methyl, so the tertiary alcohol bears three methyl groups on the carbinol carbon.
questions.hint: Two from the ketone plus one added.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the carbonyl carbon electrophilic?

answer.exemplar: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbon-oxygen double bond is polarized with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on carbon; in addition, the pi bond can accept electrons into the pi-star orbital, making carbon the site of nucleophilic attack.

questions.explanation: Polarization puts positive character on carbon. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbon-oxygen double bond is polarized with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on carbon; in addition, the pi bond can accept electrons into the pi-star orbital, making carbon the site of nucleophilic attack.
questions.hint: The pi bond is a good electron acceptor.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain acid catalysis and water removal
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does acetal formation require acid catalysis and removal of water?

answer.exemplar: Acid catalysis protonates the carbonyl and makes it more susceptible to alcohol attack, while removal of water shifts the equilibrium toward the acetal because water is a product; without water removal the reverse hydrolysis competes strongly.

questions.explanation: Acid activates the carbonyl; removing water drives equilibrium forward.
questions.hint: Acetals hydrolyze in aqueous acid.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why do primary amines give imines while secondary amines give enamines?

answer.exemplar: A primary amine has two N-H bonds and can lose both hydrogens alongside the carbonyl oxygen to form a carbon-nitrogen double bond; a secondary amine has only one N-H, so after condensation it cannot form an imine and instead loses a proton from the alpha carbon to give an alkene adjacent to nitrogen.

questions.explanation: N-H count decides imine versus enamine. A primary amine has two N-H bonds and can lose both hydrogens alongside the carbonyl oxygen to form a carbon-nitrogen double bond; a secondary amine has only one N-H, so after condensation it cannot form an imine and instead loses a proton from the alpha carbon to give an alkene adjacent to nitrogen.
questions.hint: Condensation needs two N-H hydrogens for an imine.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is the Wittig reaction useful for placing an alkene at a specific position?

answer.exemplar: The alkene forms between the former carbonyl carbon and the ylide carbon, so the double bond position is fixed by the structure of the carbonyl compound and the ylide; unlike elimination, there is no rearrangement or regiochemical ambiguity.

questions.explanation: The new double bond joins two known carbons. The alkene forms between the former carbonyl carbon and the ylide carbon, so the double bond position is fixed by the structure of the carbonyl compound and the ylide; unlike elimination, there is no rearrangement or regiochemical ambiguity.
questions.hint: No shifting or mixtures occur.

enolate formation requires base

questions.stem: A laboratory report asks: which conditions favor formation of the kinetic enolate?

options.misconception: that favors the thermodynamic enolate
that may not form the enolate fully
acid does not give lithium enolates

questions.explanation: A bulky strong base such as LDA at low temperature removes the most accessible alpha proton quickly, giving the kinetic enolate, whereas equilibrating conditions favor the more substituted thermodynamic enolate.
questions.hint: Bulky and cold gives kinetic control.

questions.stem: In the laboratory (example), what class of compound is prepared by alkylation of diethyl malonate followed by hydrolysis and decarboxylation?

questions.stem: While planning the experiment, which statement about keto-enol tautomerism is correct?

options.text: The enol is always more stable
options.misconception: most simple enols are less stable

options.text: The keto form usually predominates for simple ketones

options.text: The equilibrium is catalyzed only by strong acid

questions.explanation: For simple carbonyl compounds the keto tautomer is favored because the carbon-oxygen double bond is stronger than the carbon-carbon double bond of the enol, though enols can be stabilized by conjugation or hydrogen bonding.

questions.stem: In a research note, why does heating an aldol product favor dehydration?

options.misconception: water is formed but conjugation is the driver
the carbonyl is retained
